section.title: Complex numbers and polar form
section.p: Polar coordinates describe a point by distance and angle. Complex numbers give another way to do the same thing.
At first this looks like notation. Then multiplication reveals the surprise.
In ordinary coordinates, multiplying two points does not make sense. In complex coordinates, multiplying two points means:
section.md: \text{multiply the distances and add the angles.}
section.p: That is why complex numbers are so useful for rotation and oscillation.

exercise.title: How is a complex number a point in the plane?

statement.p: The number a+bi is pictured as the point (a,b). In your own words, why does that identification make polar coordinates a natural language for complex numbers, and what do modulus and argument measure?

hint.p: Distance from the origin is the modulus. Angle from the positive real axis is the argument. Those are exactly polar coordinates.

subsection.title: Multiplication as scaling and rotation
subsection.p: The real advantage of polar form appears when we multiply.
So multiplication by a complex number has two geometric effects:

exercise.title: What geometric meaning does complex multiplication have?

statement.p: In polar form, moduli multiply and arguments add. In your own words, why does that make multiplication by a complex number a combination of scaling and rotation, and what special motion does multiplication by i produce?

hint.p: Multiplying distances scales; adding angles rotates. The number i has modulus 1 and argument \pi/2, so it rotates by a right angle without changing size.

statement.p: The number i has polar form
Its modulus is 1, and its angle is \pi/2. Therefore multiplying by i rotates a point by 90^\circ counterclockwise without changing its distance from the origin.
That is exactly a 90^\circ counterclockwise rotation.

figure.caption: Multiplication by i rotates the plane by 90^\circ counterclockwise.

exercise.title: What does Euler’s formula put into exponential notation?

statement.p: The formula e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta places the unit circle in exponential language. In your own words, why is that compatible with the law e^A e^B=e^{A+B}, and what famous points on the circle fall out immediately?

hint.p: Adding exponents adds angles, which is how rotations compose. In particular, e^{i\pi}=-1 and e^{i\pi/2}=i.

subsection.p: This is a bridge, not a new requirement for the rest of the chapter. But it shows where the story is going.

Parametric curves taught us to let time move a point in the plane. Polar coordinates taught us to measure that point by radius and angle. Complex numbers show that the same plane can be treated as a number system, where multiplication rotates.
The proof of Euler’s formula still waits. To prove it, we need a new kind of infinite process: not an infinite area, but an infinite sum of functions.

exercise.title: Why are complex exponentials useful for oscillation?

statement.p: The equation x''+\omega^2 x=0 has sine and cosine solutions, which complex notation packages as e^{i\omega t}. In your own words, what computational convenience does that packaging provide, and why is this a bridge rather than a new requirement for the chapter?

hint.p: Differentiation becomes multiplication by i\omega. The same plane is being treated as a number system whose multiplication rotates.
